system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 59-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and HIV presented with a partially dislodged right femoral dialysis catheter, preventing her scheduled dialysis. She also reported nontraumatic pain in her left first and second toes. Imaging showed no fracture, and the pain was managed symptomatically. The dialysis catheter was successfully exchanged over the wire the night of admission without complications. Hemodialysis was completed the following day, and she was discharged home in stable condition. She was counseled on the importance of adhering to her HIV medication regimen, though she expressed a preference to take her medications at home. Follow-up was advised for persistent toe pain and routine care with her primary and specialty providers.
problems: Mechanical complication of other vascular device, implant, and graft
Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status

INDICATION:  ___ female with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. 
Right tunneled hemodialysis line discontinued for infection.  New left
tunneled femoral line and venogram requested based on worsening lower
extremity edema.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (resident), Dr. ___ (fellow) and Dr.
___ (attending, present and supervising throughout).

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
fentanyl (250 mcg) and Versed (4 mg) over a total intraservice time of 1 hour
and 15 minutes, during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
monitored continuously by an independent radiology nurse.  1% lidocaine and
lidocaine with epinephrine were administered to the skin and subcutaneous
tissues for local anesthesia.

RADIATION:  85 mGy, 17 minutes.

CONTRAST:  60 mL Optiray.

PROCEDURES:

1.  Left common femoral venous access under ultrasound guidance.

2.  Left common iliac and IVC venography.

3.  Placement of a tunneled HD catheter via the left femoral vein.

PROCEDURE DETAIL:  After discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to
the procedure, written informed consent was obtained.  The patient was brought
to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The left
groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  A preprocedure
timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ protocol.

Using a combination of fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, the left common
femoral vein was accessed with a 19-gauge needle.  A ___ wire was then
advanced through the needle into the lower IVC.  A small skin ___ was made
over the needle which was then removed.  A 5 ___ sheath was then advanced
over the wire into the left common iliac vein.  Subsequently, a venogram was
performed with findings described below.  Next, a 0.035 Glidewire was advanced
through the sheath and multiple attempts were made with the assistance of both
an Omniflush catheter and a C2 Cobra Glide catheter to cannulate the right
common iliac vein, but a decision was made to turn our attention back to
placement of the tunneled line due to patient discomfort.  

The Glidewire was advanced into the right atrium and the appropriate
measurements were taken.  After additional local anesthesia, a 1 cm skin
incision was made on the left upper thigh approximately 8 cm from the
venotomy.  A 15.5 ___ tunneled catheter was passed from the incision to the
venotomy site with the aid of a metal tunneling device.  The venotomy tract
was then dilated with 12- and ___ dilators.  A peel-away sheath was
passed over the wire.  The wire and inner cannula were removed and the
catheter was passed through the peel-away sheath.  The peel-away sheath was
then removed while the catheter was pushed into the right atrium.  This was
confirmed by fluoroscopy demonstrating the catheter tip in the right atrium. 
Both lumens aspirated blood and flushed easily.  The catheter was secured with
two 0 silk sutures.  The venotomy site was closed with a ___ Vicryl
subcuticular stitch.  Dry sterile dressings were applied.  There was no
immediate complication.

FINDINGS: Flow obstruction in the IVC / confluence of the iliac veins with
multiple collaterals.  Filling of the right common iliac via collaterals. 
Filling defect at the the right common iliac vein just proximal to the
confluence consistent with either clot or stenosis. Inability to cross this
area of stenosis with a guidewire coming over the iliac confluence, consistent
with stenosis. A more detailed venogram could not be completed due to the
patient's discomfort, and will require general anesthesia on a future visit. 

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated left common iliac and IVC venograms and placement
of a tunneled hemodialysis catheter via the left common femoral vein.  The tip
is located in the right atrium and the catheter is ready for use.

To clarify, the tip of the left common femoral vein dialysis catheter was
positioned in the mid right atrium under real time fluoroscopic guidance.

INDICATION:  ___ female with end-stage renal disease on dialysis with
complicated access history and concern for IVC stenosis on prior tunneled line
placement.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PHYSICIANS: Dr. ___ (fellow) and Dr. ___ (attending, present
and supervising throughout).

ANESTHESIA/MEDICATIONS:  General anesthesia was induced. Heparin was
administered prior to balloon plasty, 3000 units.  

RADIATION:  599 mGy, 34 minutes 9 seconds.

CONTRAST:  230 cc IV Optiray.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Right and left common femoral vein access.
2.  Bilateral common iliac venography and IVC venography.
3.  Balloon plasty via bilateral accesses in the IVC up to 14 mm.
4.  Post-balloon plasty venograms.
5.  Replacement of the existing left femoral tunneled catheter with a new 55cm
15.5F tunneled hemodialysis catheter.

PROCEDURE DETAIL: After discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to
the procedure, written informed consent was obtained.  The patient was brought
to the Angiography Suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  A
preprocedure timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ protocol.  The
bilateral groins and the indwelling left tunneled catheter were prepped and
draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Under ultrasound guidance, the patent and compressible right common femoral
vein was accessed using a micropuncture needle.  An 0.018 nitinol wire was
advanced into the common iliac vein under fluoroscopic guidance.  A small skin
incision was made and the needle was removed and exchanged for a micropuncture
sheath.  The inner portion of the sheath and the wire were removed and a
___ wire was advanced through the micropuncture sheath.A ___ vascular
sheath was then placed.  

Next, the left tunneled groin line was aspirated and flushed.  An Amplatz wire
was then advanced through one of the lumens and the tunneled catheter was
easily removed.  A 12 ___ sheath was advanced through the tunnel into the
common iliac vein with good hemostasis.  Next, an Omniflush catheter was
advanced over the wire into the lower IVC and a venogram was performed
demonstrating a 2cm segment of marked (85-90%) caval stenosis at the level of
the suprarenal IVC with extensive right perinephric and perlilumbar
collaterals. The Omniflush catheter was advanced further into the IVC and a
second venogram was performed demonstrating brisk flow above the level of the
renal veins.  

Next, we turned our attention to the right groin access.    A venogram was
performed demonstrating multiple pelvic collaterals arising from the right
common iliac vein and again a caval stenosis was again noted.  At this time, a
decision was made to perform angioplasty of the IVC. Systemic heparin was
administered. Sequential venoplasty was performed via the left femoral access
with 8mm 10 mm, 12 mm and 14 mm balloons.  There was a slight persistent waist
in the mid IVC with a 14-mm balloon however further inflation was not
possible.  Subsequently, a venogram was repeated on the right and demonstrated
preferential flow from the right common iliac through a collateral that then
joined the right renal vein and reconstituted through a collateral to the IVC.
A decision was made to repeat balloon plasty via the right common femoral
access through the entire IVC and proximal aspect of the common iliac vein
with a 12-mm balloon.  

A final cavogram demonstrated improvef flow through the IVC following plasty

Finally, we removed the sheath on the left and placed a 16 ___ peel-away
sheath through which a new hemodialysis catheter was threaded over the wire
into the IVC.  The peel-away sheath was removed and the catheter was advanced
over the wire until the tip was positioned in the right atrium.  The wire was
removed.  Both lumens aspirated and flushed easily.
A cavogram performed with the dialysis catheter in situ however showed partial
occlussion of the stenotic IVC by the 15.5F dialysis catheter.  The catheter
was secured to the skin with ___ silk sutures.  A dry sterile dressing was
applied.  The right femoral sheath was removed and manual compression was held
for 10 minutes for optimal hemostasis.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complication and
was transported immediately to the PACU.

FINDINGS:

1.  Marked caval stenosis up to approximately 90%, with a linear channel in
the IVC suggestive of a pericatheter fibrin sheath.

2.  Balloon plasty of the IVC to 14 mm with improved flow but slight residual
waste at the level just above the renal veins.
    Despite considearble improvement following balloon plasty , the presence
of a partially occlussive dialysis catheter across the stenosis means there
remains a significant  flow impedement across the IVC

3.  15.5 ___ hemodialysis catheter via the left common femoral approach.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Bilateral common iliac and IVC venography demonstrating a tight (90%)
caval stenosis and extensive right perinephric and pelvic collateralization. 
Uncomplicated IVC balloon plasty to 14mm with good angiogaphic result prior to
replacement of the dialysis catheter. Cavogram with the catheter in situ
however shows persistent , short, flow limiting stenosis at the level of
suprarenal IVC. 

2.  Replacement of the existing 15.5 ___ tunneled hemodialysis catheter in
the left common femoral vein with a new 15.5 ___ catheter via the existing
tract.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of some concerns with your dialysis line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been feeling chills and noticed pus coming from my line in the groin. It’s been sore and warm to touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you went to dialysis earlier today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they ran it slower than usual. Gave me vancomycin too. But I still felt off, so they sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’re concerned your dialysis line might be infected. We’ve sent blood cultures and checked your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve had this line for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. Infections in dialysis lines can spread. But we’re on it. We’ll start antibiotics and likely need to remove and replace the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… okay. Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use local anesthesia. You’ll be sedated a bit. It’s usually well tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having this burning when I feel like I need to pee, and more vaginal discharge. Not like a yeast infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We’ll check that too. We’ll do a swab to rule out infections like BV or STIs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sexually active, so I didn’t think it mattered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It still matters. Vaginal changes can happen due to other reasons, especially with your health history. We’ll treat it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT scan for your abdominal pain. It didn’t show anything urgent, but we’re still watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain started near the line and goes down my belly. Could it be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Infections can cause referred pain. We’ll manage it with pain meds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures haven’t grown anything yet, but the catheter tip grew MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA? Isn’t that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. The line is out, and you’re on vancomycin. That’s effective against MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on antibiotics for a while?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, four weeks of vancomycin during your dialysis sessions. We’ll monitor your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my new line is in the left groin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, placed yesterday. We made sure the vein was open. You’ll use that for dialysis going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vaginal swabs came back negative for yeast, BV, chlamydia, and gonorrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it still burns and itches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a single dose of diflucan just in case. Since tests are negative, it might be irritation. See your PCP for a Pap soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ll call my son to set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood cultures are negative. That’s good — no ongoing bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks like it. We’ll keep going as planned. Also, your echocardiogram was normal — no heart infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My heart’s been okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a venogram yesterday. Found a narrowing in the big vein in your belly — the IVC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that cause problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might affect dialysis flow. We did a balloon to open it, but it’s still a bit tight. We may need to try again later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: With another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, under general anesthesia. For now, your new line is working, and dialysis ran smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is low but stable. And your eosinophils are still high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been going on for a while. Is it from my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re checking for parasites like strongyloides. Also, an allergist might help figure it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been scratching a lot. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the skin lesions and itching could be from that. We’ve added hydroxyzine for relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue vancomycin with each dialysis. Keep the line site clean. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your HIV meds, blood pressure pills, and now we’re adding midodrine for low BP during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to pick that up last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send it to your pharmacy. It should help you feel better during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last update: your line tip is in the right spot — mid right atrium. Good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the narrowing in the vein?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still a concern, but the balloon helped. We’ll follow up with vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV? My CD4 was really low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, CD4 was 27. That’s why it’s so important to stay on your meds. We’ve continued your full regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll take them at home like I did before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. They help keep your immune system strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you this evening if your vitals stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your follow-ups — dermatology, PCP, and vascular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to. And call my son to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe and keep that line clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember — if you develop fever, chills, or swelling at the site, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll watch for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll send your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’ve done well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re medically ready too. We’ll arrange transport.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your PTH is high. Keep taking cinacalcet for your bones and parathyroid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s all for now. Rest up at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 59-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and HIV presented with chills, pain, and purulent drainage from her right femoral tunneled dialysis catheter, concerning for infection. She also reported new vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain. Blood cultures were negative, but the catheter tip grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), confirming infection. The infected catheter was removed and replaced with a new left femoral tunneled catheter. She was treated with a four-week course of vancomycin administered during dialysis. A venogram revealed IVC stenosis, which was partially treated with balloon plasty. Vaginal swabs were negative for infections, and symptoms were managed with a single dose of fluconazole. Her HIV was managed with continued antiretroviral therapy, and her low CD4 count was noted. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue antibiotics, resume midodrine for dialysis-related hypotension, and follow up with her PCP, dermatology, and vascular surgery.
problems: Bloodstream infection due to central venous catheter
Other complications due to renal dialysis device, implant, and graft
